automata.title: Finite Automata
automata.description: Study deterministic and non-deterministic finite automata. Build DFAs and NFAs, convert regular grammars, and step through input words.
automata.tutorialQuestion1: What is the difference between deterministic and non-deterministic finite automata (DFA vs. NFA)?
automata.tutorialAnswer1: A DFA has exactly one next state for each state and input symbol. An NFA allows zero, one, or multiple next states as well as ε-transitions.
automata.tutorialQuestion2: When does a finite automaton accept an input word?
automata.tutorialAnswer2: An input word is accepted if the automaton ends in at least one accepting state after completely reading all symbols.
automata.tutorialQuestion3: How are the transition table and state diagram connected?
automata.tutorialAnswer3: The transition table provides the formal definition of state transitions, while the state diagram graphically visualizes the active execution path.
automata.overviewText: Finite Automata are the simplest computational models used to recognize patterns. They consist of states, transitions, and accept/reject decisions. DFAs and NFAs form the foundation for lexical analysis, pattern matching, and regular expression engines.

number.title: Number Systems
number.description: Master conversions between Binary, Octal, Decimal, and Hexadecimal. Understand IEEE 754 floating-point representation.
number.overviewText: Number systems are fundamental to how computers store and process data. Understanding binary, octal, and hexadecimal representations is essential for low-level programming, networking, and digital design.
number.tutorialQuestion1: What are the most important number systems in computer science?
number.tutorialAnswer1: The most important number systems are binary (base 2), octal (base 8), decimal (base 10), and hexadecimal (base 16).
number.tutorialQuestion2: Why is the binary system so important for computers?
number.tutorialAnswer2: Computers are based on electronic circuits that primarily know two states: on (1) and off (0).
number.tutorialQuestion3: How are decimal numbers converted to binary numbers?
number.tutorialAnswer3: You repeatedly divide the decimal number by 2 and note the remainder (0 or 1), which, read from bottom to top, gives the binary number.

encoding.title: Encoding
encoding.description: Learn Base64 and UTF-8 encoding. Understand how text is converted to Base64 strings and how characters are represented as UTF-8 byte sequences.
encoding.overviewText: Encoding schemes like Base64 and UTF-8 are fundamental to how data is transmitted and stored. Base64 converts binary data to ASCII-safe text, while UTF-8 provides a universal character encoding that supports all writing systems.
encoding.tutorialQuestion1: What is Base64 encoding and why is it used?
encoding.tutorialAnswer1: Base64 encodes binary data into ASCII characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /). It is used to safely transmit binary data over text-based protocols like email (MIME) or JSON, where only printable ASCII characters are allowed.
encoding.tutorialQuestion2: How does UTF-8 encode Unicode characters?
encoding.tutorialAnswer2: UTF-8 encodes each Unicode code point in 1 to 4 bytes. ASCII characters (U+0000-U+007F) use 1 byte, preserving compatibility with ASCII. Non-ASCII characters use 2-4 bytes with a specific bit pattern: 110xxxxx for 2-byte, 1110xxxx for 3-byte, and 11110xxx for 4-byte sequences.
encoding.tutorialQuestion3: What is the difference between encoding and encryption?
encoding.tutorialAnswer3: Encoding transforms data into a different format for compatibility (e.g., Base64, UTF-8) and is reversible without a key. Encryption transforms data to keep it secret and requires a secret key to reverse (e.g., AES, RSA). Encoding provides no security, while encryption does.

turnstile.title: Turnstile control
turnstile.description: Model a turnstile as a Moore machine with states LOCKED and UNLOCKED. COIN unlocks a locked turnstile and leaves an unlocked one unchanged. PASS locks an unlocked turnstile and has no effect while locked. Outputs are 0/LOCKED and 1/FREE. Complete the transition and output tables, binary encodings, encoded tables, and state diagram.

elevator.title: Elevator control
elevator.description: Model a two-floor elevator with states EG_CLOSED, EG_OPEN, OG_CLOSED, and OG_OPEN. OPEN and CLOSE control the door. GO_OG and GO_EG move the elevator only while the door is closed; movement commands have no effect while it is open. Complete the Moore transition table and state diagram.

barrier.title: Parking garage barrier
barrier.description: Model a parking garage barrier with an always-open guest mode and a card-controlled mode. In card mode, VALID_CARD opens the barrier and PASS closes it after the induction loop detects the vehicle. Rework the behavior as a Moore machine and define suitable state-dependent output actions.

vending.title: Vending machine
vending.description: Model a vending machine accepting 50-cent and 1-euro coins for drinks costing 1.00 and 1.50 euros. START has no effect below 1 euro, extra coins at 1.50 euros are returned, and CANCEL returns the full credit. Determine events and actions, handle every event in every state, mark the initial state, and express the behavior as a Moore machine.

wiper.title: Windshield wiper control
wiper.description: Develop a Moore control system for windshield wipers with off, single-wipe, continuous, and rain-sensor modes. Driver controls and the rain signal are events. Define state-dependent motor outputs for stopping, wiping once, and continuous wiping, then complete the state diagram.

alarm.title: Alarm system
alarm.description: Model an alarm system with OFF, ARMED, and ALARM states. ON arms the system, the door sensor triggers a continuous alarm only while armed, and OFF switches the system off and stops an active alarm. Define the initial state, complete all transitions, and add suitable Moore outputs.

cruise.title: Cruise control
cruise.description: Model simplified cruise control with OFF, READY, and ACTIVE states. ON_OFF controls power, SET activates regulation, braking or accelerating deactivates it, RESET resumes the stored speed, CANCEL deactivates it, and PLUS/MINUS adjust the speed while active. Abstract from the concrete speed value and define suitable Moore outputs.

moore.title: Moore & Mealy Machines
moore.description: Explore sequential circuit design with Moore and Mealy state machines. Learn the differences and when to apply each model.
moore.overviewText: Moore and Mealy machines are finite state machines with output. In Moore machines, output depends only on the current state. In Mealy machines, output depends on both the current state and the current input. Both are fundamental to digital circuit design.
moore.tutorialQuestion1: When is a machine a Moore machine?
moore.tutorialAnswer1: In a Moore machine, the output depends only on the current state. The output is attached to the state and changes only after a state transition.
moore.tutorialQuestion2: What makes a Mealy machine different?
moore.tutorialAnswer2: In a Mealy machine, the output depends on the current state and the input symbol being read. The output is attached directly to the transition.
moore.tutorialAnswer3: First check where the output is defined. When converting Mealy to Moore, states often need to be split so each output belongs unambiguously to one state.

dnf.title: Disjunctive Normal Form
dnf.description: Learn how boolean expressions are evaluated with truth tables and how the Disjunctive Normal Form is derived from the rows with result 1.
dnf.overviewText: Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF) writes a boolean expression as OR-linked AND terms. In the lecture style, each truth-table row with result 1 contributes exactly one term.
dnf.tutorialAnswer1: A DNF is an OR of AND terms. The terms consist of variables or their negations and do not always have to contain every variable.
dnf.tutorialQuestion2: How is the canonical DNF derived from a truth table?
dnf.tutorialAnswer2: An AND term is formed for each row with result 1. Variables with value 1 stay positive, while variables with value 0 are negated. Because every term contains all variables, it describes exactly one table row. The terms are then joined with OR.
dnf.tutorialQuestion3: What is the difference between canonical and minimal DNF?
dnf.tutorialAnswer3: The canonical DNF contains one complete minterm for every 1-row. The minimal DNF combines compatible minterms and describes the same function with as few literals as possible.

algebra.title: Boolean algebra rules
algebra.intro: These rules let you rewrite a DNF into shorter equivalent forms. They power the step-by-step solution path and the worked examples in the simulator.

identity.name: Identity
identity.example: 1 acts as the neutral element of ∧ and 0 as the neutral element of ∨.

domination.name: Domination
domination.example: Whatever is OR-ed with 1 is forced to 1; whatever is AND-ed with 0 is forced to 0.

idempotence.name: Idempotence
idempotence.example: Repeating the same operand neither tightens nor relaxes the term.

double_negation.name: Double negation
double_negation.example: Two negations cancel each other out.

complement.name: Complement
complement.example: A variable is always either true or false — so a ∨ ¬a is always 1, and a ∧ ¬a is always 0.

commutativity.name: Commutativity
commutativity.example: Operand order does not affect the result for ∧ and ∨.

associativity.name: Associativity
associativity.example: With multiple ∧ or ∨ operations, the grouping does not matter — (a ∧ b) ∧ c equals a ∧ (b ∧ c).

distributivity.name: Distributivity
distributivity.example: A shared operand can be factored out — like factoring in regular maths, but with ∧ and ∨ instead of · and +.

absorption.name: Absorption
absorption.example: If a is already true, then a ∨ (a ∧ b) is also true — the AND part adds nothing.

de_morgan.name: De Morgan
de_morgan.example: Negation flips the operator: ∧ becomes ∨ and each operand is negated.

java.title: Java Programming
java.description: Work with core Java basics such as console output, loops, and arrays. The simulation tab provides a directly editable Java code editor.
java.overviewText: This topic introduces simple Java programs step by step. The focus is on the Main class, the main method, console output, loops, and small array-based tasks.
java.tutorialQuestion1: Why do I need the main method?
java.tutorialAnswer1: The main method is the entry point of a simple Java program. When you run the program, Java starts executing the first statement there.
java.tutorialQuestion2: How do I print text to the console?
java.tutorialAnswer2: System.out.println writes one line to the console. It is useful for showing intermediate results and testing small programs.
java.tutorialQuestion3: When do I use loops and arrays?
java.tutorialAnswer3: Loops repeat statements, while arrays store multiple values under one name. Together they help you process lists of data systematically.

java.example2Text: A for loop is the standard way to repeat the same instruction several times.

loops.description: for, while, do/while, and for-each work for exercises and small algorithms.

arraysCollections.title: Arrays, lists, maps, and sets
arraysCollections.description: Arrays and typical java.util collections work: Arrays.sort, ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, HashSet, Collections.sort.

objects.title: Own types
objects.description: Custom classes, constructors, enums, records, interfaces, and static methods can be placed in the same editor file.

output.title: Console output
output.description: Output is captured and shown in stdout or stderr below the editor.

standardLibrary.title: Standard library subset
standardLibrary.description: Common library classes from java.lang, java.util, java.math, and simple java.time are available. OS-facing APIs are not reliable.

singleFile.title: One editor file
singleFile.description: The UI currently sends one source file. Put helper classes into the same file instead of using a multi-file project.

input.title: Console input
input.description: The input box supports simple declarations using Scanner.nextLine() and Scanner.nextInt(). Values are substituted into the source before compilation; a real interactive System.in stream and BufferedReader are not supported.

cli.title: Terminal commands
cli.description: The editor expects Java source code, not commands. java, javac, jshell, jar, mvn, and gradle are not executed as terminal commands.

environment.title: OS access
environment.description: Local files, sockets, started processes, and native libraries are blocked by the browser runtime model.

runtimeFeatures.title: Dynamic runtime features
runtimeFeatures.description: Reflection-heavy code, dynamic class loading, and real Java threads are not reliable in this WebAssembly target.

stringsMath.title: Strings, Math, and big numbers
stringsMath.description: StringBuilder, String methods, Math functions, BigInteger, and BigDecimal work for typical console tasks.

run.title: Compile and run the current editor content
run.description: The Run button sends the Java source to the browser compiler, generates WebAssembly, and executes the Main.main method in the worker.

compile.title: Compilation is available as part of Run
compile.description: The internal compiler command uses javac diagnostics and TeaVM code generation. The UI does not expose a separate standalone compile-only terminal command.

javaCli.title: No java command-line launcher
javaCli.description: Typing or expecting a local java command is not supported because the browser environment does not start JVM processes.

javacCli.title: No javac terminal command
javacCli.description: javac is embedded inside the browser compiler pipeline. Users cannot pass arbitrary javac flags or compile multiple project files from a local directory.

jshell.title: No interactive JShell
jshell.description: The simulator executes complete programs with a Main class. It does not provide a REPL or interactive command prompt.

tools.title: No packaging or documentation tools
tools.description: Tools such as jar, javadoc, Maven, Gradle, and other local executables are outside the supported browser compiler workflow.

stdin.title: Console input is not interactive
stdin.description: Scanner.nextLine() and Scanner.nextInt() use the fixed simulator input box. Other Scanner methods, BufferedReader, and input during execution are not supported.

environment.title: Browser sandbox restrictions apply
environment.description: Programs should avoid local files, sockets, native libraries, process execution, and environment-dependent APIs because WebAssembly runs inside a browser worker.

addition.desc: Positional addition in binary. Adding two ones creates a carry to the next position.

subtraction.step3: 3. Add the two's complement to Number A
subtraction.carryOutInfo: Since we subtract via two's complement, a carry-out usually means the result is positive. We just discard the carry in this fixed-point system.

multiplication.stepDesc: Bit {{n}} ({{bit}}) = 1, so multiplicand {{val}} shifted left by {{shift}} = {{result}}

division.desc: Written division by trial (go from left to right).
division.stepDesc: Step {{n}}: {{current}} >= {{divisor}}, so 1 to quotient and subtract {{divisor}}

shifting.desc: Here you can shift binary numbers to the left or right.

shifting.shiftRightExpl: A right shift by n positions corresponds to a division by 2^n (without remainder).

shifting.rightStepsTitle: Right Shift: Bits fall off on the right

shifting.stepRightComplete: All {{count}} right bits have been removed.

ieee754.expAligned: Now both operands have the exponent 2^{{exp}} and can be added (or subtracted).
ieee754.normBack: The result is converted back into the format 1.M × 2^E.
ieee754.shiftDesc: The mantissa of the smaller number is shifted to the right by {{diff}} places.
ieee754.addDesc: Now both operands have the exponent 2^{{exp}} and can be added.
ieee754.normDesc: The result is converted back into the format 1.M × 2^E.

compare.padDesc: The numbers are padded to the same length (with leading zeros):

compare.stepResultLess: At position {{pos}}: A has 0, B has 1 → A is less than B.

topic.title: Turing Machines
topic.description: Learn about the fundamentals of computation through Turing Machines and their transition functions. Explore the limits of what can be computed.

overview.overviewText: A Turing Machine is a mathematical model of computation that defines an abstract machine which manipulates symbols on a strip of tape according to a table of rules. It provides a simple yet powerful framework for understanding what problems can be solved algorithmically.

exercises.exerciseWorksheetAlternatingSymbolsDesc: Given a binary word over {0, 1}, construct a Turing machine that checks whether 0 and 1 always alternate, halting as soon as two equal symbols follow each other or the end of the input is reached.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSwapFirstTwoSymbolsDesc: Construct a Turing machine that swaps the first two input symbols, leaves all remaining symbols unchanged, and finishes on the third symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSetFirstAndLastToOne: Set First and Last Symbol to 1
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSetFirstAndLastToOneDes: Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the first and last input symbols with 1, leaves all other symbols unchanged, and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetAlternatingOverwriteDes: Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the input from left to right with alternating 0 and 1 symbols and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetOverwriteLastTwoWithZer: Set the Last Two Symbols to 0
Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the last two input symbols with 0 and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetAsciiParityBitDesc: Given an input of exactly seven bits, construct a Turing machine that counts the number of ones, writes the even-parity bit to the blank cell left of the input, and finishes on the first blank cell after the input.
exercises.exerciseEraseTapeDesc: Build a machine that replaces the whole input word with blanks and halts once the tape is cleared.
exercises.exerciseInvertBinaryWordDesc: Build a machine that flips every 0 to 1 and every 1 to 0, then halts on the first blank cell.
exercises.exerciseUnaryIncrementDesc: Build a machine that appends one additional 1 to the end of a unary word and then halts.
exercises.exerciseDuplicateZerosDesc: Construct a Turing machine that doubles the number of 0s on the tape when they are enclosed by two 1s. Examples: 101 -> 1001, 1001 -> 100001.
exercises.exerciseAddBinaryDesc: Construct a Turing machine that is able to add two numbers in binary representation. To simplify the task, you may make assumptions. For example, you may define that the first addend (the left one) is greater than the second addend, that the read head always starts on the first input symbol, or that a specific symbol must appear between the numbers.
exercises.exerciseCheckRegexDesc: Given the regular expression R1 = (1(01)* | 0(10)*) construct a Turing machine that checks whether an arbitrary binary word can be described by R1. After execution, the tape must contain either a 't' for true or an 'f' for false. Example: The input 11001 cannot be represented by R1, so the tape contains an 'f' and everything else has been removed.
exercises.exerciseBinaryIncrementDesc: Build a machine that adds 1 to a binary number on the tape and halts with the incremented result.

examples.example1Desc: A complete machine that inverts every bit in a binary word while scanning from left to right.
examples.example2Desc: A compact machine that scans to the end of a unary word and writes one extra 1.
examples.example3Desc: A carry-based machine that increments a binary word by one.
examples.example4Desc: A complete binary-adder machine for inputs such as 101+11. Follow the tape states and transitions to see how the second addend is consumed and the result is built.
examples.example5Desc: Search for two consecutive zeros and then write E. Example: The input ⋄1001⋄ produces the output ⋄100E⋄.
examples.example6Desc: The tape contains a finite sequence of 0s and 1s bounded by ⋄ on both sides. Search for three consecutive zeros, write E after them, and halt. The head then rests on the symbol to the left of E. If the pattern is not found, the machine stops on ⋄. Example: ⋄10000⋄ becomes ⋄1000E⋄.
examples.example7Desc: Under the same conditions, search for the pattern 010, write E after it, and halt with the head on the symbol to the left of E. Example: ⋄10100⋄ becomes ⋄1010E⋄. The inputs 0010 and 00010 also contain the pattern.

buildFromScratch.description: Start with a blank canvas and create your own DFA or NFA from scratch. Add states, define the alphabet, and build transitions step by step.
buildFromScratch.hint: You can switch between DFA and NFA mode at any time in the editor.

examplesTab.title: Predefined Examples
examplesTab.subtitle: Learn how finite automata work by studying these examples. Each one includes a step-by-step explanation of how and why it was built.

exercisesTab.title: Practice Exercises
exercisesTab.subtitle: Build each automaton yourself. Use hints if you get stuck — full solutions only if you ask.

endsWith01.title: Strings ending with "01"
endsWith01.goal: Build a DFA that accepts binary strings ending with "01".
endsWith01.description: Design a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts exactly those strings whose last two symbols are "0" followed by "1" (e.g. "01", "101", "1001"). Strings ending in any other pattern must be rejected.

endsWith00.title: Strings ending with "00"
endsWith00.goal: Build a DFA that accepts binary strings ending with two zeros.
endsWith00.description: Design a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts exactly those strings whose last two symbols are both 0 (e.g. "00", "100", "1100"). Single zeros or strings ending in 1 must be rejected.

evenOnes.title: Even number of 1s
evenOnes.goal: Accept binary strings containing an even number of 1s (including zero 1s).
evenOnes.description: Design a DFA that tracks the parity of 1s seen so far. The empty string should be accepted (zero is even).

noConsecOnes.title: No two consecutive 1s
noConsecOnes.goal: Accept binary strings that never contain "11" as a substring.
noConsecOnes.description: Design a DFA that rejects any string in which two 1s appear next to each other. Strings like "0", "01", "010" are accepted; "11", "0110" are rejected.

divBy3.title: Binary numbers divisible by 3
divBy3.goal: Accept binary strings whose decimal value is divisible by 3.
divBy3.description: Build a DFA that tracks the running remainder of the binary value modulo 3. Accept the states representing remainder 0.

grammarTwoOnesZeros.title: Automaton from Grammar: 11 0ⁿ
grammarTwoOnesZeros.goal: Build a DFA for the language L = { 11 0ⁿ | n ≥ 0 }: two ones followed by any number of zeros.
grammarTwoOnesZeros.description: Construct a DFA that accepts exactly the words derived by the right-linear grammar shown below, then check whether the word "11001" belongs to the language.

grammarOnes.title: Automaton from Grammar: 1 0ⁿ 1
grammarOnes.goal: Build a DFA for the language generated by the grammar below.
grammarOnes.description: Construct a DFA that accepts exactly the words derived by this right-linear grammar. Each non-terminal becomes a state; the ε-production marks an accepting state.

grammar0011.title: Automaton from Grammar: (0011)(0011)*
grammar0011.goal: Build a DFA for the language generated by the grammar below.
grammar0011.description: Construct a DFA that accepts exactly the words derived by this right-linear grammar. Each non-terminal becomes a state; the ε-production marks an accepting state.

rl.title: Regular Languages
rl.description: Work with regular languages and their right-linear grammars — enumerate the words generated by a grammar, derive a grammar from a language definition, and test word membership.
rl.tutorialAnswer1: A right-linear grammar contains only productions of the form A -> aB, A -> a, or A -> ε. It generates regular languages.
rl.tutorialQuestion2: How are regular grammars connected to finite automata?
rl.tutorialAnswer2: Every right-linear grammar can be converted directly into an equivalent finite automaton (non-terminals become states) and vice versa.
rl.tutorialQuestion3: How is word membership in a regular language checked?
rl.tutorialAnswer3: Either by step-by-step derivation from the start symbol of the grammar, or by simulating the word through the corresponding finite automaton.
rl.overviewText: A regular language is a set of words that can be described by a regular grammar or a finite automaton. This module focuses on right-linear (Type 3) grammars.
rl.feature1: Enumerate the language generated by a grammar up to a maximum word length
rl.feature2: Generate a grammar from a word enumeration or set-builder notation
rl.feature3: Check whether a word belongs to the language generated by a grammar
